name: More Volume, Same Pipes: Why 2025–2026 Broke the Spread Machine Open
deck: Three simultaneous demand booms—GLP-1 drug adoption, AI hardware buildout, and infrastructure construction—flooded existing distribution and infrastructure platforms without spawning competing intermediaries, allowing fixed-capacity spread machines to extract outsized margin growth.
core_bet: In 2025-2026, three unrelated volume surges hit distribution and infrastructure platforms simultaneously: GLP-1 drug adoption accelerated pharmaceutical flows; AI data-center buildout pulled electrical, power, and cooling components; and infrastructure reshoring/grid buildout consumed pipe, cable, and generation assets. None of these booms created new intermediaries—they just flooded the existing platforms (Arrow, WESCO, Cencora, Energy Transfer) at higher utilization. Fixed-capacity distribution networks extracted outsized margin growth because supply could not elastically scale. Arrow components revenue jumped 39% YoY, WESCO data-center sales rose 45% YoY, Energy Transfer raised guidance 31% (EBITDA guidance from $17.45B to $18.8B), and Cencora absorbed GLP-1 volume growth while managing specialty-margin expansion.

mechanism: Distribution intermediaries like Arrow, WESCO, and Cencora operate on a classic spread-machine model: they buy products from suppliers at wholesale, hold inventory at risk, and sell to end-customers at retail spread. The margin is small (1-3% of sales) but repeatable. The model depends on volume velocity and inventory turns—move $30B in products through the system at 2% margin, and you earn $600M. The challenge is that margins compress if supply exceeds demand (customers can bypass the intermediary, suppliers can direct-distribute), or if demand shocks overwhelm existing infrastructure (leading to cost and capital requirements that erase margin gains).

In 2025-2026, three volume surges hit intermediary platforms at the same time without creating new competing pipes: GLP-1 drug adoption accelerated sharply (Cencora managing higher pharma flows without new competitors entering the distribution layer); AI data-center buildout pulled electrical, power, and cooling components at unprecedented scale (Arrow and WESCO seeing AI-linked demand that existing customers needed from existing suppliers); and infrastructure reshoring plus grid buildout consumed energy infrastructure (Energy Transfer's Q2 2026 showed midstream gathered volumes up 4%, NGL exports up 25%, NGL transportation up 13%, all feeding into the same pipe system). These are not overlapping booms in the same market; they are simultaneous booms in separate markets that all feed through the same distribution and infrastructure choke points.

The result is that intermediaries with fixed capacity extracted outsized spread because they could not lose volume to competitors, and customers could not bypass the system. Arrow's components revenue rose 39% while operating leverage stayed modest (nonGAAP operating income fell 5.3% YoY despite 39% revenue growth) because high demand pulled through inventory faster than margins could expand. WESCO data-center sales rose 45% while the company explicitly said backlog was up 60% to record levels—indicating that the company was constrained, not that it was harvesting existing capacity with ease. Energy Transfer's adjusted EBITDA guidance raise from $18.2B-$18.6B to $18.8B-$19.1B ($500M midpoint increase) was driven by contract wins, export loading, and volume growth, not margin expansion. Cencora's GLP-1 flows were lower-margin than specialty pharmaceuticals, yet the company grew revenue 4.9-5.9% even while absorbing that mix pressure. The spread machine works by taking whatever volume comes through and extracting consistent spreads; 2025-2026 simply showed extreme volume without new competition to split the margin.

The deeper insight is that the three booms did not spawn competing intermediaries. GLP-1 adoption did not create new pharma distributors—Cencora, Cardinal Health, and McKesson still control 90%+ of U.S. drug distribution. AI data-center buildout did not create new electronics distributors—Arrow and Avnet still dominate component distribution. Infrastructure reshoring did not create new pipeline operators—Kinder Morgan, Energy Transfer, and Williams still control the corridor choke points. The intermediaries operate on fixed physical assets (distribution centers, pipeline miles, inventory capacity) that take years to build and billions to deploy. When new demand appears, customers must source from existing intermediaries at existing spreads. This is why the 2025-2026 period broke spread machines open: volume surged against fixed capacity, margins stayed intact because there were no new entrants, and adjusted EBITDA guidance jumped without any corresponding investment in new infrastructure.
why_now: The volume surge is happening now because three technology and demand waves are peaking simultaneously in ways that have not aligned before. GLP-1 adoption accelerated from niche to mainstream in 2025-2026 (Ozempic/Mounjaro volume, generic-version launches, insurance coverage expansion). AI data-center buildout moved from announcement to physical construction phase in 2025-2026 (hyperscalers committing capital, electrical and power infrastructure becoming the binding constraint). Infrastructure construction and reshoring accelerated with bi-partisan policy support, grid-reliability concerns, and offshoring-reversal incentives through 2025-2026. All three needed to pull through physical supply chains at the same time. None of them could create new distribution or infrastructure systems in one year. The result is that intermediaries saw 30-45% volume growth hitting 2-3% margin spreads, resulting in 20-30% bottom-line earnings acceleration even without operating leverage.
who_pays: End consumers pay higher prices for pharmaceuticals (Cencora absorbs some GLP-1 margin dilution but passes cost through system), data-center customers pay higher prices for electrical and power infrastructure (WESCO's 60% backlog indicates supply constraints pushing pricing up), energy end-users pay higher transport and storage fees (Energy Transfer raising EBITDA guidance on volume growth, not price expansion). Suppliers also face pressure to provide products through limited intermediaries without alternative distribution channels. The cost is highest for customers who cannot negotiate around the intermediary or who depend on immediate supply from existing inventory.
who_profits: Distribution and infrastructure intermediaries: Arrow, WESCO, Cencora, Energy Transfer, Kinder Morgan, and Williams all see earnings accelerate from volume rather than margin expansion. The spread machine captures value by being the only viable routing for urgent volume. Shareholders in these companies benefit from operating leverage at existing cost structures. Some suppliers benefit if they can expand volume through existing relationships without adding new sales or service infrastructure.
tension: The spread-machine model breaks when competing intermediaries enter the market or when customers bypass the system. In 2025-2026, neither happened—new entrants take years to build (pipeline operators, distribution centers), and customers cannot self-source faster than existing intermediaries move volume. But the model also breaks if volume disappears as quickly as it appeared. If GLP-1 adoption plateaus, if AI data-center buildout slows (leading to inventory clearances and reduced component demand), or if infrastructure projects pause, these intermediaries will be left with the same fixed costs supporting lower volume. The margin spreads will compress as utilization falls. Energy Transfer already suspended Lake Charles LNG because it did not believe long-term LNG export demand justified the capex; that is a signal that management sees limits to the volume surge.
surprising_part: The most striking aspect is that the volume surge did not create operating leverage at these intermediaries—it just validated that they own the choke points. Arrow's revenue up 39% but operating income up only 7%; WESCO growing backlog 60% but still managing margin pressure from digital-transformation costs; Energy Transfer raising EBITDA guidance by $500M but still carrying leverage concerns. These are not hyper-profitable spreads; they are efficient choke-point operations moving more volume through the same infrastructure. The earnings acceleration comes from velocity, not from pricing power or margin expansion. This matters because it shows how much value a spread machine captures simply by being the unavoidable intermediary, not by being the best operator.
one_sentence: Three simultaneous demand booms flooded fixed-capacity distribution and infrastructure intermediaries without spawning new competitors, allowing spread machines to extract outsized margin growth without operational improvement.
societal_stake: This is about who controls the physical supply chains underneath new technology waves and what they charge for that control. GLP-1 distribution, AI infrastructure delivery, and grid modernization are all hitting consumers through intermediary markups and pricing power. If these volume booms are temporary (GLP-1 adoption plateaus, data-center construction slows), intermediaries will be left with excess capacity and will have to compete more aggressively on price. Consumers will benefit from cheaper access. But if the booms are structural (GLP-1 becomes a standard-of-care medication, AI infrastructure is permanently capacity-constrained, grid buildout continues for decades), intermediaries will lock in pricing power and consumers will pay the accumulated spread for decades. The outcome depends on whether new competitors can build capacity fast enough to break the choke point.
